coldOpen.title: THE RIDE
coldOpen.note: Four cards, face down. Turn one at a time and let each hook land in silence; the fuller lines, to say aloud if you like: At the edge of a forest, a researcher has ten years of data and one urgent question. / In a village square, a community worker has 300 families to reach before dark. / In a room full of files, a data lead guards records that could save lives, or expose them. / By a broken bridge, a tech worker is stuck with a tool nobody can fix. Then the last line under the cards. The engine idles underneath; mute it from Sound if the room is loud.
coldOpen.lineYou: Your choices decide how they get there.

lines: Too cautious costs time and fuel now.
Shortcuts save time now, and leave a loose bolt that breaks later.
The first step rarely costs you. The choices after it do.
rules.note: One screen, short. Point at the clock and fuel bill on the lead motorcycle: they stay on screen all the way.

bolt1.label: Alert sent only to the three villages
bolt1.message: Remember the alert sent straight to the three villages? Those were simply the villages with mobile signal. The real hotspot had no reports, and cattle were lost there last night.

bolt2.label: An alert app launched in a week
bolt2.message: The alert app? Half the families couldn't install it, and the rest lost signal after dark. We turn back to set up voice calls.

bolt3.label: Records uploaded with only names removed
bolt3.message: Remember uploading the records without names? Age, village and diagnosis together pointed to one mother. Her family found out from a report. We stop to repair the damage and the trust.

bolt4.label: Launched before the notes were written
bolt4.message: The tool stopped working on the way in, and the notes were never written. Nobody can log in.

stops.voice: Before we set off, someone shared a website with us. It made us stop and look twice.

steps.note: Click the website (or press →) to bring it up full screen. Scroll with the mouse wheel or ↓ ↑. Then ask who built it.

steps.question: Who do you think built this?

options.text: A web agency
An experienced developer
A small tech team
Someone with no coding background, using AI

steps.note: A quick guess, not a question. Lock it, then reveal who built them.
steps.revealNote: No development team built it. The hard part has moved from writing code to choosing the right problem.

steps.question: We could build something with AI this weekend. How do we start?

options.text: Build a rough version this weekend to test one idea
options.outcome: Off to a flying start. Something real on the screen gets real feedback fast.

options.text: Pick one real problem first, then build a small test
options.outcome: A short pause to name the problem. Now we know exactly what we're looking for.

options.text: Spend weeks mapping every feature and stakeholder first
options.outcome: Still at the workbench while the road waits. Planning for weeks before touching anything burns time and energy.

steps.text: AI makes trying things cheap. Knowing which problem you're trying to solve keeps it useful.

stops.handover: If the hard part is the problem, let's go where the problems are.

stops.voice: I have ten years of camera-trap photos and notes on cattle lost to tigers. I want to know where the next attack is likely, before it happens.

steps.context: AI studies her data and points to three villages.
steps.question: AI points to three villages. What's our move?

options.text: Send the alert to those three villages tonight
options.outcome: Alert sent, 30 minutes saved. For now. Keep an eye on that bolt.

options.text: Go through Meera's field notes and the quiet, unrecorded areas first
options.outcome: Meera spots it: two villages barely appear in the records. The alert goes where it's needed.

options.text: Quick check-in with the three villages and two low-signal neighbours
options.outcome: Fast and grounded. The quick check-in turns up a missed hotspot next door.

options.text: Set the AI aside and stick to the old paper logs
options.outcome: Safe, but slow. Hours of useful pattern-spotting left on the table.

steps.text: AI only sees the data that reached it. Silence in the data can mean missing signal, not safety. Fast pattern-spotting plus people who know the ground is the winning pair.

stops.handover: Even if the warning is right, it's useless if it doesn't reach people. Lakshmi knows how.

stops.voice: When a warning comes, I have to reach 300 families. Half have basic phones, many can't read, and the signal drops after dark.

steps.question: How do we get the warning to these families?

options.text: Voice messages through channels families already use
options.outcome: Fast because it fits: familiar voices on the phones people already have.

options.text: Launch an alert app this week
options.outcome: The app is live, 30 minutes saved. Do you hear that rattle?

options.text: Test voice messages with 10 families first, in their own dialect
options.outcome: Ten families later, Lakshmi knows the words that land and the time of day people pick up.

options.text: Survey all 300 families before sending anything
options.outcome: A thorough survey, while the warning waits. Sometimes over-studying is its own risk.

steps.text: Accessibility is language, literacy, devices and signal. Technology works best when it bends to people's lives.

stops.handover: To reach families, I keep names, phone numbers and addresses. Arif deals with that every day.

steps.title: On the road to Nagpur
steps.prompt: How are we doing? Which choice is costing us the most?
steps.line: Look at the fuel bill. The shortcuts felt free when we took them. This is where they start costing.
steps.lineNoBolts: Look at the fuel bill. No shortcuts so far, so nothing has come loose.
steps.note: A pause to reflect, no vote. Say it: “Look at the fuel bill. The shortcuts felt free when we took them. This is where they start costing.” (or, with no shortcuts: “Look at the fuel bill. No shortcuts so far, so nothing has come loose.”). Then ask which choice is costing the most, and whether any loose bolts were worth it.

stops.voice: We have records for 40 clinics. AI could spot which mothers are at risk before it's too late. But every record has a name, a phone number and a diagnosis.

steps.question: How do we let AI look at these records?

options.text: Remove names and numbers, share only what the question needs, and keep the key that links them back safe at home
options.outcome: Slower by half an hour, and the mothers who need care are found without exposing anyone.

options.text: Remove names and numbers, then upload the rest
options.outcome: Names gone, analysis running, 30 minutes saved. That bolt looks loose.

options.text: Lock everything away and test nothing
options.outcome: Nothing exposed, and nothing learned. The mothers who needed early care are still invisible.

steps.title: Swap names for tokens
steps.text: AI works with the tokens. The key that links them back stays with you. It lowers the risk, it doesn't erase it.
steps.note: Tokenised is not the same as anonymous. Whoever holds the key can link it back.

steps.text: Removing names isn't enough. Share only what the question needs, and guard what can lead back to a person.

steps.title: Insight Out by Tech4Good
steps.text: Questions like these are what Insight Out explores: making AI useful for social-impact work while taking data, privacy and infrastructure seriously.
steps.note: Point people to Insight Out if they want to take these questions further.

stops.handover: Whatever we set up, someone has to keep it running. Ravi knows what happens when nobody does.

stops.voice: Two years ago, a college team built us an app for crop prices. They graduated. Now it's broken, nobody has the password, and farmers still call me about it.

steps.question: Our tool is working. What do we do before moving on?

options.text: Shared logins, plain notes and a named owner, then launch
options.outcome: Thorough. Anyone in the team can pick this up tomorrow.

options.text: Launch now, and write the notes once it's stable
options.outcome: Launched, 30 minutes ahead. Who has the password?

options.text: Keep it simple: basic notes, a shared login and a monthly check-in
options.outcome: Light and practical. It'll still be standing months from now.

steps.text: Launching is a moment. Keeping it running is a habit.

steps.title: Trip ledger
steps.subtitle: This room's run
steps.note: Read out the arrival time and the fuel bill, then the bolts.
The room's own route is the bright line.

steps.question: Looking at the optimal route, which ONE habit does your team want to bring into its work?

options.text: Choosing clear, real problems before building
Checking ground reality and keeping tools accessible
Protecting people's information and earning trust
Keeping tools documented, shared and easy to maintain

steps.resultLine: The habit this room is taking home.

steps.text: No single formula: move fast where it's simple, pause where it matters, don't play it too safe.
steps.signoff: See you on the next convoy.
steps.note: Talk it through, one phrase at a time. The full version: We left Bengaluru and arrived at Travancore Palace. The ride shows there's no single formula. Sometimes moving fast and simple wins. Sometimes a short pause to check the ground, protect someone's information or write a few notes saves hours and rupees later. And playing it too safe costs you too. The best route pairs smart tools with human judgement, care and steady upkeep, and we travel it better together. Nobody gets here alone.
lines: Move fast where it's simple. Pause where it matters.
Smart tools, human judgement, steady upkeep.
